newsitem.title: BURUNDI: UN refugee chief pleased with Zaire rebel pledge.
newsitem.headline: UN refugee chief pleased with Zaire rebel pledge.

text.p: U.N. refugee chief Sadako Ogata arrived on Monday in Burundi after welcoming a promise by east Zairean rebels to avoid a camp of more than 127,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees.
Ogata told reporters she came to Bujumbura on the third leg of her African mission to secure guarantees for the security of Burundian Hutu refugees repatriated from neighbouring Tanzania.
The Tutsi-dominated Burundian army, which is at war with Hutu rebels, has admitted killing 126 Burundian Hutu refugees in one incident in January after they were forced out of Tanzania.

Following the killings, Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, appealed to Tanzania to halt the deportations. More than 20,000 Burundians fled from Burundi to Tanzania last month, joining 36,000 who fled in December and 98,000 in November.
Speaking in Nairobi earlier on Monday, Ogata said: "I was very pleased with the response that (rebel leader Laurent) Kabila said he was not going to attack the Tingi Tingi camp."
Kabila, fighting to overthrow President Mobutu Sese Seko, said on Saturday his forces would avoid Tingi Tingi and move towards eastern Zaire's largest city Kisangani, 200 km (125 miles) northwest.
The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire has reached Amisi, 70 km (45 miles) south of the camp, driving thousands more refugees towards Tingi Tingi.
The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda in 1994 because of fears of reprisals for a genocide of minority Tutsis by hardline Hutus.
Following attacks on their camps in eastern Zaire in November last year, some fled west into the Zairean jungle and more than 600,000 returned home, trekking in the opposite direction.
Tingi Tingi is the largest single grouping of refugees in eastern Zaire, but UNHCR officials say the location of more than 200,000 Rwandan refugees scattered by fighting is unclear.

Ogata visited Tingi Tingi and Kinshasa at the weekend and said agreement had been reached with the Zairean government on the principle of repatriating the remaining Hutus. She appealed for them to be given safe passage to return home to Rwanda.
"To get safe passage assured I think requires a lot more talking (with the rebels)," she told a Nairobi news conference.
But even before a pact on repatriation is reached with the rebels there is deep doubt over how many refugees, who marched for weeks to escape Kabila's Rwandan-backed fighters, want to go home.
Among them are soldiers of the Hutu-dominated former army and Interahamwe militiamen who took part in the 1994 genocide.
Some of the Hutus are fighting alongside Mobutu's ragged army and foreign mercenaries he hired to counter the rebels.
"The grip of the Interahamwe and former army was a very strong factor in preventing the refugees' return," Ogata said.
"What is going to be their position as they flee further west I don't know, but I think there will be people who do not want to go back."
